title: Bret Hart
wiki_lead:
Bret Sergeant Hart (born July 2, 1957) is a Canadian and American retired professional wrestler. A member of the Hart wrestling family and a second-generation wrestler, he has an amateur wrestling background at Ernest Manning High School and Mount Royal College. A major international draw within professional wrestling, he is credited with changing the perception of mainstream North American professional wrestling in the early-mid 1990s by bringing technical wrestling to the fore. He is widely regarded as one of the greatest professional wrestlers of all time; Sky Sports noted that his legacy is that of "one of, if not the greatest, to have ever graced the squared circle". For the majority of his career, he used the nickname "the Hitman".
Hart joined his father Stu Hart's promotion Stampede Wrestling in 1976 as a referee and made his in-ring debut in 1978. He gained championship success during the 1980s and 1990s in the World Wrestling Federation (WWF, now WWE), where he helmed the Hart Foundation stable and was the face of company's New Generation Era. He left for World Championship Wrestling (WCW) following the controversial "Montreal Screwjob" in November 1997, where he remained until October 2000. Having been inactive from in-ring competition since January 2000, owing to a December 1999 concussion, he officially retired in October 2000, shortly after his departure from the company. He returned to sporadic in-ring competition from 2010 to 2011 with WWE, where he won his final championship, headlined the 2010 SummerSlam event, and served as the general manager of Raw. Throughout his career, he headlined the respective premier events of the WWF and WCW, WrestleMania (9, 10, and 12) and Starrcade (in 1999). He was inducted into the Wrestling Observer Newsletter Hall of Fame upon its inception in 1996, while still an active performer.
Hart held championship titles in five decades from the 1970s to the 2010s, 32 throughout his career and 17 between the WWF/WWE and WCW. Among other accolades, he is a seven-time world champion; a five-time WWF Champion and a two-time WCW World Heavyweight Champion. He went the most combined days as WWF Champion during the 1990s (654) and was the first WCW World Heavyweight Champion born outside the United States. He is the second WWF Triple Crown Champion and fifth (with Goldberg) WCW Triple Crown Champion. He is also the 1994 Royal Rumble match winner (with Lex Luger), and the only two-time King of the Ring, winning the 1991 tournament and the first King of the Ring pay-per-view in 1993. He co-headlined multiple pay-per-view events as part of an acclaimed rivalry with Stone Cold Steve Austin from 1996 to 1997. He is the first wrestler to be inducted three times into the WWE Hall of Fame: in 2006 individually, in 2019 as a member of the Hart Foundation, and in 2025 when his Submission match with Stone Cold Steve Austin at WrestleMania 13 was inducted as the inaugural entry into the Immortal Moments category.
Outside of wrestling, Hart has appeared in numerous films and television shows such as The Simpsons as well as featuring in several documentaries, both about himself specifically and others about his family or the wrestling industry in general. He also helped found and lent his name to the major junior ice hockey team the Calgary Hitmen and has written two biographies along with a weekly column for the Calgary Sun for over a decade. After his retirement, he spent much of his time on charitable efforts concerning stroke recovery and cancer awareness, due to his experiences with the two.

grok_lead: Bret Sergeant Hart (born July 2, 1957), better known by the ring name Bret "The Hitman" Hart, is a retired Canadian professional wrestler, author, and actor renowned for his exceptional technical wrestling prowess and as a pivotal figure in the Hart wrestling dynasty. Widely regarded as one of the greatest in-ring performers in professional wrestling history, he achieved prominence in the World Wrestling Federation (WWF, now WWE) during the 1980s and 1990s, where he captured the WWF World Heavyweight Championship five times and became synonymous with precision, storytelling, and the slogan "the best there is, the best there was, and the best there ever will be." Born in Calgary, Alberta, as the eighth of twelve children to wrestling promoter and patriarch Stu Hart and his wife Helen, Bret grew up immersed in the sport through his family's promotion, Stampede Wrestling. From a young age, he trained rigorously in the Hart family's underground facility known as "the Dungeon," a notoriously grueling space that honed his skills alongside his brothers and other relatives, including future wrestlers Owen Hart and brother-in-law Jim Neidhart (the British Bulldog). After earning accolades in amateur wrestling during his youth, including provincial championships in Alberta, Hart transitioned to professional wrestling in the late 1970s, debuting for Stampede Wrestling where he won multiple titles and gained experience touring internationally in Japan and Europe. Hart's major breakthrough came in 1984 when he signed with the WWF, initially teaming with his brother-in-law Jim "The Anvil" Neidhart to form the Hart Foundation tag team, which dominated the division by securing the WWF Tag Team Championship twiceâfirst in 1987 and again in 1990. Transitioning to singles competition in the early 1990s, he solidified his status as a main event star, capturing the WWF Intercontinental Championship twice (in 1991 against Mr. Perfect and in 1992 at WrestleMania VIII against Roddy Piper) before embarking on a record-setting run as a five-time WWF Champion, with victories over legends like Ric Flair (1992), Yokozuna (1994 at WrestleMania X), and Diesel (1995). His matches, often lauded for their athleticism and narrative depth, included the iconic 60-minute Iron Man Match against Shawn Michaels at WrestleMania XII in 1996, which he lost in sudden-death overtime, and his 1993 King of the Ring victory, cementing his "Excellence of Execution" moniker. A defining and controversial moment in Hart's career occurred at Survivor Series 1997 in Montreal, Quebec, known as the "Montreal Screwjob," where WWF owner Vince McMahon orchestrated a surprise title loss to Shawn Michaels without Hart's knowledge or consent, as Hart was contractually bound to depart for World Championship Wrestling (WCW) amid a dispute over his WWF contract. This incident fueled a real-life rift with McMahon and the WWF, leading Hart to join WCW in 1998, where he won the WCW World Heavyweight Championship twice and the WCW United States Heavyweight Championship once. His WCW tenure, however, was marred by creative frustrations and culminated in a career-ending injuryâa severe concussion from a kick by Bill Goldberg in December 1999âprompting his retirement in 2000 at age 42. Post-retirement, Hart faced further health challenges, including a debilitating stroke in 2002 from which he remarkably recovered through intensive rehabilitation, regaining much of his mobility and speech. He reconciled with WWE in 2010, returning for high-profile appearances, including defeating McMahon in a No Holds Barred match at WrestleMania XXVI and inducting family members into the Hall of Fame. Hart has since pursued writing, authoring the bestselling autobiography Hitman: My Real Life in the Cartoon World of Wrestling in 2007, and acting in projects like the TV series Lonesome Dove: The Outlaw Years, for which he earned a Gemini Award nomination, and stage productions such as Aladdin: The Magical Family Musical. A two-time WWE Hall of Famerâindividually in 2006 and with the Hart Foundation in 2019âwho inducted his brother Owen in 2022, he remains a Canadian icon, honored as one of the nation's top 50 greatest citizens by CBC in 2004, and continues charitable work while advocating for wrestling's legitimacy.
